ON THE LAW OF WAR

III. For first, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the mere reason of the thing due to his own action) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither is the thing itself with him, nor does he hold any gain from the thing.

<margin>Covar. to ch. "peccatum," part II, § 1; Silv. on the word "Restitut." n. 3, qu. 6.</margin>

<margin>Medina on contracts, qu. 10.</margin>

IV. Secondly, a possessor in good faith is held to restore also the fruits <note>meaning the profits or products</note> existing from the thing: I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the owner of the thing. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership. For he who is the owner of the thing is naturally also the owner of the fruits of the thing.

<margin>Zeff. b. II, ch. 14; Navar. ch. 17, n. 7.</margin>

V. Thirdly, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much in any other case: for in this, he is considered to have been enriched. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised near the beginnings of his reign, because to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he added also the fruits of the intervening time.

<margin>Suet. ch. 16.</margin>

VI. Fourthly, he is not held to the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifthly, if such a possessor has given to another a thing that was given to him, he is not held unless he would have given just as much even without this thing: for then there will be a profit in having spared his own property.

<margin>L. "Quivas," § last, D. of theft.</margin>

VIII. Sixthly, if he has sold a thing he bought, he is not held, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sold a thing that was given to him, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>L. "Si & rem," D. concerning the petition of an inheritance.</margin>

IX. Seventhly, a thing of another bought in good faith must be restored, and the price paid cannot be demanded back. To this rule, it seems to me that an exception should be added, unless insofar as the owner could not have recovered possession of his thing without some expense, for instance, if the thing had been with pirates. For then it will be possible to deduct how much the owner would have willingly spent. For the possession of the deed itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something estimable, and in this, the owner is considered to have been enriched after the loss of the thing. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own thing is not valid under ordinary law, nevertheless, Paul the jurist says it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession, which is with another, be purchased. Nor do I require here that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action for the management of business <term>negotiorum actio</term> arises.

<summary>This page outlines the legal obligations of a good-faith possessor regarding restitution of property and its profits, including exceptions for cases involving potential expense for recovery, such as dealing with pirates.</summary>
